## Module 3 in two minutes

**A CEO asks who owns AI and gets six confident, different answers.** Nobody is lying and nobody is wrong, AI isn't a function, it lands inside every function at once, so each executive can see the piece that is genuinely theirs. Which means **confidence in that room tells you nothing.**

**So it gets settled by precedent rather than principle**, and a scope question decided by default is decided against the function that wasn't present `[V]`. In 52% of organizations HR has no direct involvement in AI strategy at all.

**The strongest available argument is narrow.** If agents have owners, budgets, access rights, performance standards, onboarding and offboarding. That is workforce management, and every one of those is a discipline your function already has and no other executive does.

**And the strongest objection is that the analogy flatters you** `[V]`. Agents are software; the disciplines that transfer are infrastructure ones others already do well. **Winning could be the worst outcome** — acquiring operating-system overhead exactly when Module 2 said your attention should move out of it.

## The test

**Does your claim start with "HR owns…" or with "No system may…"?**

The first requires you to win on authority, in a room where five other people have an equally good claim. The second requires someone to argue out loud that a review is unnecessary. The synthesis that survives is usually **a named decision right rather than ownership**: no agent deployed into a process affecting a person's work, pay, evaluation or access without your sign-off.

## What the full module adds

Why "AI is fundamentally about people" loses, and what demonstrated competence looks like instead. **The decline in three parts** (what you aren't claiming, what you require anyway, and what you do instead) which is a legitimate answer that serious CPOs choose, and which is only absence when the three parts are missing. **The already-decided case**: when the CIO has selected the vendor and you're handed adoption, relitigating loses and *claiming the consequences* usually wins, because nobody else wants them. Four claims to judge, only one of which gets what it asks for. And the activity: three sentences, plus **the limit, what you would refuse even if it were offered.**
